regenerable_on: a guest running kea-dhcp4 with a control socket the capture user can reach. THREE collections, not four: lease4-get-all ships in libdhcp_lease_cmds and this guest loads no hooks, so the leases collection has no interface here at all — se-capture-guest asks the daemon for list-commands and captures the lease payload only where the command is offered, so a re-stage on a hook-loaded guest opens four. The daemon's uptime, its pid and the statistic sample timestamps move on every re-stage, and the Uptime anchor below is re-read by hand in the same change or it is asserting a machine that is gone.
anonymisation_note:
Substituted, not merely gated: this is the first capture in the corpus whose native document carries a machine's own hardware address. harness/scrub/kea.json classifies by what each member carries on ANY host rather than by what this one happens to hold, so the reservation identifiers (a hw-address, three client-ids, a DUID and a flex-id), every reservation address, the pool range, and every operator-chosen name (the DDNS prefix, the client-class name, two server-hostnames, one client hostname) were all rewritten. The independent detectors were run over the raw payloads first and reported six findings — the MAC by its registered OUI and five named hosts — and over the committed bytes afterwards and reported none.

Two scrub artefacts are stated rather than left to be discovered. `arguments.hash` is Kea's SHA-256 over its own configuration and now covers a document that no longer exists, so it and the committed config disagree by construction. And the pool RANGE was substituted endpoint by endpoint while `subnet[1].total-addresses` was not — a counter is a number and nothing correlates it back to the range it counted — so the pool reads 192.0.2.5-192.0.2.210 (206 addresses) beside a total of 200. Neither is read by the collector, which takes its totals from the statistics document and never parses the range.

The one member the gate forced to `nothing` is the subnet CIDR, and the manifest's #bound-subnet entry says why: 192.0.2.0/24 is the documentation range this scrubber substitutes INTO, so a /24 there is a fixed point and no rule can engage. Declared location/ipv4 it was refused, correctly. A capture from a host with a real subnet must reclassify it first.
note:
The DIRECTORY is `no-lease-hook` and the variant kind is `healthy`, and both are true: this Kea is answering, its subnet is configured and nothing about it is degraded — what it does not have is the lease-commands hook, which is the one thing a reader needs to know before wondering where the fourth collection went. The corpus already spells directories that way (network/fedora-empty declares kind empty-ruleset, network/debian-absent declares absent). It is ALSO the name that made the pair land, which is worth writing down rather than leaving as a coincidence: seeded under `kea/healthy` the issuance collided with storage/spare-engaged on generation 235, and test_no_two_variants_issue_the_same_generation refuses that. The collision is a property of a stateless hash over a growing corpus — 895 possible bases, nineteen variants, seventeen apart — and not of this variant, so the next collector will meet it too and rename its way out of it in the same way until the issuance is made injective over the corpus rather than over a seed string.

One DHCP server, five documents, THREE collections — and the collections are not one per document. `daemon` joins version-get to status-get; `subnets` joins statistic-get-all to config-get; `reservations` folds config-get alone. A port that published a row per document, or that keyed a collection on the command, gets different commit counts from the same payloads.

What this variant does NOT stage, and each is a shape a reader might otherwise assume was covered:

· `leases` has no payload here. lease4-get-all is a hook command (libdhcp_lease_cmds) and this guest loads no hooks, so the command is not offered — list-commands is committed beside the others precisely so that claim is evidence a reviewer can check rather than a sentence in this note. corpus/README's coverage report carries the named residual (`kea/leases`), and the whole ExpiresAt/State/lease-row derivation is exercised by no replayed stream.

· No shared-networks. Every subnet here is declared at the top level, so `_subnet_scopes`'s second arm — a subnet declared INSIDE a shared network, whose statistics exist under subnet[id] whether or not the walker finds it — is unvisited. A walker that read only Dhcp4.subnet4 would produce this exact stream. That is the shape the adapter's own docstring calls absence masked as a healthy row, and no committed capture can see it.

· No global reservations, so `reservation:global/<ip>` is minted by nothing here, and every reservation carries a Subnet fact.

· Every reservation states an ip-address, so UnlistedReservations is absent and ReservationCount equals the number of rows. The anchor below asserts that absence rather than leaving it implied.

· `ip-reservations-unique` is true, so no address carries two reservations and `_disambiguated` passes every id through untouched. The hw-address and ordinal fallbacks it exists for are unexercised.

· never-send is false on every option, so the suppression marker that must mask a wider scope's value is never set; and no option is declared at shared-network scope, so the middle rung of the three-scope merge is empty. What IS exercised is the outer pair: DnsServers comes from the GLOBAL option-data and Routers from the SUBNET's, in one row, so a port that read only one scope loses one fact and keeps the other.

· The pool is empty — nothing has ever leased from it — so AssignedAddresses, DeclinedAddresses and UsedPercent are all zero. They are anchored as READINGS, not absences: a port that dropped zero-valued facts as uninteresting fails, and so does one that computed UsedPercent only when assigned > 0.

· The socket answered, so no failure path is staged. absent, unauthorised and unavailable — no socket configured, a socket whose group this collector is not in, a socket with nothing listening — are three statements the collector must make and this variant makes none of them.

· No names family, no absent list, no unobservable record and no relation assertion: every fact these documents can state is present, so the three non-value channels are unvisited.

The configuration is Ubuntu's shipped kea-dhcp4.conf example, unmodified, which is why one subnet with six reservations covers as many reservation identifier KINDS as it does — hw-address, client-id, DUID and flex-id all appear, and the adapter reads exactly one of them.
anchors_note:
Read off payloads/version-get.json, payloads/status-get.json, payloads/statistic-get-all.json and payloads/config-get.json by hand at staging, before any stream existed, and every one of them was then corrupted in the payload and watched to fail — an anchor nobody has seen fail is a claim, not an authority.

The objects are named by the row's NATIVE name, which is different in all three collections and is not the object id. `kea-dhcp4` is the daemon's, `192.0.2.0/24` is the subnet's CIDR (the adapter falls back to the bare subnet id only where the config states no CIDR, which is the shared-network blindness this variant cannot stage), and a reservation's is its IP ADDRESS — never `reservation:1/192.0.2.145`, which is the id the adapter mints and the collator re-derives from the declared prefix.

Version 3.0.3 comes from version-get's `text` and not from `arguments.extended`, which begins with the same characters and continues into the linked library list. A port that published the extended string carries the OpenSSL build date into a fact.

Uptime 8821 is status-get's `uptime`, which on this capture EQUALS its `reload` — the daemon has not been reconfigured since it started — so the anchor cannot tell the two members apart and says so here rather than implying it can. A re-stage that reloads Kea separates them and makes this anchor discriminating; today the pid, 33392, is the only status member that could not be confused with another.

QueueDepthAverages is anchored as [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], three FLOATS. It is the only non-integer in this pair and it catches a whole class: a port that decoded the queue statistics as integers publishes [0, 0, 0], which passes an untyped comparison and fails the corpus judge's typed equality. It is also the reason the fact is a list rather than three: status-get states a moving average over the last 10, 100 and 1000 packets, and only the list says which is which.

The subnet row is anchored across BOTH its documents deliberately. SubnetId, TotalAddresses, AssignedAddresses and DeclinedAddresses come from statistic-get-all, whose values arrive as [[value, timestamp]] — the newest reading is the first element of the first sample, so a port that took samples[0] whole publishes a list and a port that took the timestamp publishes a string. Subnet, LeaseTimeSeconds, Routers, DnsServers and ReservationCount come from config-get. A port that read one document and not the other produces half this row and no fewer rows, which is why the halves are anchored separately instead of by count.

Routers and DnsServers are anchored TOGETHER and come from different scopes on purpose: Routers is the subnet's own option-data, DnsServers is the global option-data with no subnet override. A port that read only the subnet scope loses DnsServers; one that read only the global scope loses Routers; one that let the global value win over the subnet's publishes 192.0.2.5, 192.0.2.146 for Routers. Each is a different failure and the pair separates them.

UsedPercent 0, AssignedAddresses 0 and DeclinedAddresses 0 are READINGS. The pool has never been leased from, and zero is what that looks like — so a port that omitted zero-valued facts, or that computed the percentage only when something was assigned, fails these three and not the total beside them.

UnlistedReservations is anchored ABSENT and ReservationCount is 6, which is the same number as the reservations collection's commit. Every reservation here states an ip-address, so the remainder is nil and the fact is omitted rather than published as 0 — rule 7's omission, and the anchor is what stops a port publishing a helpful zero.

The reservation anchors are chosen so that each one fails for one reason. 192.0.2.145 is the ONLY reservation with a hw-address, so its HwAddress anchor is the whole of what the adapter reads from four different identifier kinds — the other five carry a client-id, a DUID or a flex-id and the adapter reads none of them, which is what the absent_fact on 192.0.2.218 pins. 192.0.2.82 is the only reservation whose hostname is not the empty string, so its Hostname anchor and the absent_fact on 192.0.2.150 are the two halves of one rule: Kea normalises an unset hostname to "" rather than dropping the member, and a port that tested for the member's presence instead of its truth publishes Hostname "" on five rows. commit_objects 6 is anchored because none of the fact anchors can see a seventh row.

Deliberately not anchored: every statistic sample TIMESTAMP, the pid, and the `reload` counter. The timestamps are readings of the clock at the moment the counters were created, no fact is lifted from them, and anchoring one would pin this pair to a wall-clock moment a re-stage cannot reproduce.
